messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

James Sullivan, a 46‑year‑old graphic designer with a calm, methodical habit, had never imagined his life would be punctuated by the flashing blue of a police cruiser. On a rainy Thursday evening in late October, while he was walking home from a late client deadline, a police officer stopped him at a crosswalk that had, according to James’s memory, been empty for months. The officer demanded that James pull over, but James, certain that he had been following the streetlights, stepped off the curb and began to walk, his hand instinctively reaching for the envelope of a design file tucked into his jacket. The officer’s knuckles pressed on the car door, his face turned from confusion to anger, and before James could even ask why he was being stopped, a hand shoved his shoulder, a sharp hiss of rubber, and a sudden, painful sting as a hand struck his face. The officer’s boots, with their dark, scuffed soles, seemed to echo the harshness of the moment. He felt a rush of fear, the kind that makes the heart pound and the vision blur, and when the siren’s wail faded into a distant drone, he was left alone on the pavement, clutching a broken smartphone screen, bruised in places he could not immediately name. From that night forward, James’s world narrowed to the images and sounds that had defined his trauma. The intrusive thought of a police officer’s glare came unbidden when he passed a courthouse, the sight of a child with a torn sleeve on a school bus triggered an immediate recollection of a hand slamming against his own arm, and the very presence of an authority figure—any uniformed person—caused his chest to tighten. These triggers did not simply remind him of the event; they lit a fire in his mind, generating a state of threat. He could not relax, no matter how far from the scene he was, and he constantly mapped escape routes in his mind before he could feel safe, even at his office. In the dim glow of his studio, with a whiteboard full of color swatches and a monitor displaying client logos, his body stayed taut, fingers on the mouse hovering, the muscles of his neck and shoulders ready to respond to a danger that never truly left. The memory of the assault seeped into his life in waves that overwhelmed him. When the memory returned, James felt so much emotion—anger, fear, humiliation—that he would freeze mid‑sentence, unable to finish explaining what had happened to anyone. He could not clearly describe the officer’s face or the exact force of the shove; the narrative tangled like a knot in his mind, leaving him feeling helpless. The mere thought that someone might not believe his version of events, that the system had failed him, seemed to make the memory even more vivid. James had begun to think that the injustice of the incident was a wound that would never heal; the idea that his life had been destroyed by a single act of violence left him feeling as if every color he ever chose was meaningless. Because of these intrusive triggers and the sense of threat that followed, James turned to maladaptive strategies that he had learned from other stressful moments. He began to spend long hours on his phone, scrolling through memes or playing endless rounds of a puzzle game, to keep his mind occupied and to avoid thinking about the officer’s hand. Whenever he felt a flash of a face or heard a siren, he would immediately pull the device out and dive into a stream of social media content, forcing the brain to stay in the present of the screen rather than the present of the past. He also started to avoid other people, refusing to join colleagues for lunch or to attend team meetings, believing that any group setting might bring up authority figures or strangers who could provoke his memories. These avoidance tactics, while offering temporary relief, only deepened the cycle. The longer he stayed in the safety of his screen, the more the memories resurfaced with intensity, and the more he felt threatened by the world outside his studio. James’s negative appraisals compounded this loop. He came to believe that his life had been irreparably damaged; that the world was a hostile place where people could strike without consequence. These beliefs did not just accompany the threat—they amplified it. When a sudden siren drifted through the office hallway, the sense of impending danger rose, and he felt the same tightness in his shoulders he had felt on that rainy night. The memory of the officer’s hand became a constant reminder that the world was unforgiving, and his attempt to escape through screen time only reinforced the perception that reality was dangerous and that he was powerless to change it. In the months that followed, the maladaptive strategies became habits. When James returned to his work, he found himself scrolling through a game for hours, his laptop screen becoming a refuge. He avoided coworkers, which strained his marriage; his wife, Maria, began to feel neglected and frustrated by his isolation. The constant tension made him anxious, and he began to dread even the sight of a police badge, fearing that a simple stop could trigger a flood of memories. By the time he reached out for help, he was exhausted, his sense of meaning extinguished, and his life seemed to have little hope of recovery. The last spark that brought him to therapy was the realization that he could no longer live on autopilot; each day he woke, he was terrified that a passing siren would snap him back into that dark, violent memory. He was most afraid that the cycle would never break, but he also clung to a fragile hope that a professional might help him untangle the tangled web of his mind and restore even a sliver of peace.
